srcs.question: Who should lead the Coalition (from a named list: Ley, Hastie, Taylor, Wilson, O'Brien)?

text: The Newspoll, which included a question asking 1245 voters who should lead the Coalition from a list featuring Ms Ley, Mr Hastie , opposition defence spokesman Angus Taylor, Deputy Opposition Leader Ted O’Brien and opposition industrial relations spokesman Tim Wilson, showed 46 per cent of Australians didn’t know who they would prefer.

Amid the speculation about Ms Ley’s long-term future, Newspoll found 21 per cent of voters preferred her as Liberal leader ahead of Mr Hastie (15 per cent), Mr Taylor (9 per cent), Mr Wilson (6 per cent) and Mr O’Brien (3 per cent).

The poll, conducted between Monday and Thursday last week as Ms Ley engaged in almost 40 media interviews and daily press conferences, revealed 28 per cent of Coalition voters preferred the Opposition Leader ahead of Mr Hastie (20 per cent) and Mr Taylor (12 per cent).

Amid fears over more rate hikes and ongoing cost-of-living pressures, almost one in two voters believe the budget will make inflation worse, compared to only 9 per cent who say it will make it better and 32 per cent who say it will make no difference. The government’s big sell on its $47bn housing program and crackdowns on negative gearing and CGT appears to have a long way to go, with just 27 per cent of voters saying the budget was a step in the right ­direction. Almost 40 per cent of voters, including those who own shares and investment properties, said Labor’s budget meant they would pay more tax overall, compared with 41 per cent who said it would make no difference, and only 7 per cent who believed they would pay less tax overall.

srcs.question: Which view is closer: 'the people who built this mess aren't going to fix it — Australian politics is overdue for a big shake-up', or 'the system looks broken until you consider the alternative — steady government has delivered prosperity'?

text: Core support for Pauline Hanson’s One Nation has surged ahead of Labor for the first time in Newspoll history, as Anthony Albanese’s popularity hit record lows and an overwhelming majority of voters ­declare Australian politics is overdue for a big shake-up.

Amid the rise of One Nation, which claimed just 6.4 per cent of the primary vote at last year’s May election, a special Newspoll question showed a majority of all voting demographics – except for Labor voters – endorsed a dramatic change in the political status quo. Almost 70 per cent of voters agreed “the people who built this mess aren’t going to fix it” and that “Australian politics is overdue for a big shake-up”.

That compares to 32 per cent of Australians who believe the system “looks broken until you consider the alternative” and that decades of steady government have delivered “prosperity that more chaotic political systems can only envy”.
